newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's recovery leaves many behind.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's recovery leaves many behind.

text.p: Laura Fernandez and her father wait patiently for a lawyer in the twilight of a dilapidated concrete office in Mexico City.

She is 42, single, and earns 2,000 pesos ($253) a month as a secretary. Dressed smartly for work, she clutches a letter from major Mexican bank Banamex demanding payment of a 57,000 peso ($7,215) credit card bill and threatening legal action.
"We can't pay in one go what they are asking," she tells the lawyer at Mexican debtors' group El Barzon (the yoke), which represents more than a million bank debtors.
A bill of 6,000 pesos ($760), manageable more than two years ago, became a monster when interest rates soared in the wake of the December 1994 peso crash.
Fernandez said she has been intimidated by 3:00 a.m. telephone threats, though Banamex denies it allows calls after 9:30 p.m. by the debt collectors it contracts.
However, she is just one of Banamex's 200,000 credit card debtors, who together with thousands more Mexico-wide are still struggling to pay for Mexico's financial crisis.

The amount of consumer debt, including credit card and durable goods loans, still owed to banks in December 1996 totalled 8 billion pesos ($1.01 billion), according to Rogelio Ramirez, director of economic advisers Ecanal.
Government subsidies via lower interest rates helped bring that down from 13 billion pesos ($1.64 billion) when the crisis broke in December 1994.

But mortgage debt over the same period has skyrocketed -- to 205 billion pesos ($26 billion) from 103 billion ($13 billion) Ramirez said -- because housing loans restructured after the crisis were indexed to consumer price inflation and therefore continued to grow.

"I calculate that about 1 million households are currently trapped in these mortgage loans," he said. "Families have been repaying their credit card and consumer loans, but housing loans are ... not being repaid."
The shock waves of the crisis are still being felt at every tourist spot and every traffic light across the city, where more street vendors vie for trade more than ever.
Jose Luis Gomez Castaneda, a lawyer for El Barzon, said the number of cases is still growing. El Barzon was set up to defend citizens' rights and fight the banks through the courts.
"The numbers are just ballooning," he said. "We have 300 to 350 court cases at the moment and the number will double in the next two months."
Ramirez agreed that housing repossessions, on hold during the run-up to mid-term elections scheduled for July, would rise steeply after the polls.
The debt overhang is one of the reasons Mexico's gradual recovery from the 1994-5 crisis has so far failed to generate any feel-good factor among ordinary people.

Government predictions of 5 percent growth and a million new jobs a year by 2000 sound hollow to thousands of households still struggling to eliminate domestic debt and recover their former standard of living.

Mexico's first quarter GDP growth came at an unspectacular 5.1 percent after 7.6 percent in the fourth quarter last year, while retail sales for the first three months showed a discouraging 3.5 percent slump.
Then came an uptick in April unemployment and a 4 percent plunge in supermarket sales, dashing hopes that a broad-based revival in domestic consumption might finally have begun to materialise.

Seasonally adjusted, the growth figures looked even less good -- just 3.9 percent for the fourth quarter of 1996 and 0.9 percent in the first quarter of this year, according to Alfredo Thorne, an economist at J.P. Morgan in Mexico City.

"The depressed level of activity created by the deep 1995 recession facilitated very high year-on-year growth rates during 1996. But these are seen to be illusory once the data are restated in seasonally adjusted terms," he said.
But other analysts say the picture is not that bleak.
A sharp decline in Mexico's April trade surplus, though it jangled the nerves of currency traders, showed a surprise increase in imports.
"It does suggest we may be seeing signs of a revival," said Denis Parisien, Vice President for Latin American Research at Bankers Trust in New York.
